Apoſtol c. 40. ſhevveth the ſette Houres of prayers, and the reaſons therof : Make your prayers Early in the morning, at the Third houre ; Sixt, Ninth ; Euening ; and at the Time of cocke crovving. Early geuing thankes becauſe our Lord hath illuminated vs, the night being paſſed, & the day coming in ; the Third, becauſe that houre our Lord receiued Pilats ſentence ; the Sixt houre, becauſe then he was Crucified ; the Ninth, becauſe al thinges were moued, when our Lord was crucified, abhorring the audacitie of the wicked, & not bearing the ignominie of our Lord ; at Euening, geuing thankes, for that God hath geuen vs the night for reſt of dayes labours : at the Cocke crowing, becauſe at that time the coming of the day is denounced, to exerciſe the workes of light, thus S. Clement. Touching the diſtinct and ſette times of publique prayer, the continual practiſe by tradition teacheth, that Mattines with Laudes were ſaid in the night, about the firſt Cockcrovving. Prime early in the morning. The other partes in the day time : At euening Euenſongue, and laſt of al Compline. And touching the place : If for the infidels (ſaith the ſame holie Father) there be not acceſſe to the Church, the Biſhop muſt geather the Aſſemblie at home, that the godlie may not enter into the Church of the wicked : for the place doth not ſanctifie man, but man the place. VVherfore if the vvicked occupie the place, that place is to be ſhunned, becauſe it is prophaned by them : for as Prieſtes do ſanctifie holie thinges, ſo the vvicked do contaminate them. If neither at home, nor in the Church Aſſemblies can be celebrated, let euerie one by himſelfe ſing, read, pray, or twoo or three be geathered together. For where twoo or three are geathered in my name (ſaith Chriſt) there am I, in the middes of them. Let not the godlie pray with an heretike, no not at home. For what ſocietie is there of light vvith darknes ?

verses.text: There is <na>(e)</na> much peace to them that loue thy law: & <na>(f)</na> there is no ſcandal to them.

notes.label: e
notes.text: Amongſt other benefites, it is a ſpecial commoditie, that thoſe which perfectly loue Gods law, haue alwayes peace in their owne conſcience :

notes.label: f
notes.text: and are neuer ſcandalized, that is, do not fal nor committe ſinne, by anie occaſion whatſoeuer geuen them by others. For it is a general aſſured doctrine, that the perfect are not ſcandalized, becauſe they are conſtant in vertue, and not moued by anie example, perſwaſion, prouocation, or other meanes to offend God : but only the weake and vnperfect are moued, and drawne to ſinne by occaſions geuen them, who otherwiſe would not haue ſinned. Neither is he excuſed that falleth by ſuch occaſions, becauſe he ought to be conſtant.

verses.text: I expected thy ſaluation ô Lord: and haue loued thy commandmentes.
My ſoule hath kept thy teſtimonies: and <na>(g)</na> hath loued them excedindgly.

notes.label: g
notes.text: Not of ſeruile feare, but of true charitie & filial loue.

verses.text: I haue kept thy commandmentes, and thy teſtimonies: <na>(h)</na> becauſe al my waies are in thy ſight.

notes.label: h
notes.text: Becauſe whatſoeuer I do is in thy ſight, whom i wil in no caſe offend.

verses.heading: Tau. Signe.
verses.text: <na>(a)</na> Let my petition approch in thy ſight ô Lord: according to thy word giue me <na>(b)</na> vnderſtanding.

notes.label: a
notes.text: In this laſt Octonarie, and concluſion of this Pſalme, the faithful ſeruant of God prayeth,

notes.label: b
notes.text: not for humane knowlege, or other temporal thinges, but to vnderſtand Gods law.

verses.text: Let my requeſt enter in thy ſight: <na>(c)</na> according to thy word <na>(d)</na> deliuer me.

notes.label: c
notes.text: Thou that haſt promiſed to heare al that inuocate thee,

notes.label: d
notes.text: voutſaffe to deliuer me in time of tribulations and tentations.

verses.text: My lippes shal vtter an hymne, when thou shalt teach me thy iuſtifications.
My tongue shal pronounce thy <na>[1]</na> word: <na>(e)</na> becauſe al thy commandmentes are equitie.

notes.label: e
notes.text: God geuing grace, it behoueth his ſeruants thankefully to ſerue, and praiſe him.
Why the 15 Pſalms following are called Gradual Canticles. Here follow in order fifteen Pſalms entitle Gradual Canticles.

verses.text: <na>(f)</na> Let thy hand be to ſaue me: becauſe I haue choſen thy commandmentes.

notes.label: f
notes.text: Though man be indued with grace, yet he nedeth more grace, that by Gods hand and powre, not by his owne, he may reſiſt tentations.

verses.text: I haue coueted thy ſaluation ô Lord: and thy law is my meditation.
<na>(g)</na> My ſoule shal liue, and shal prayſe thee: and thy iudgementes shal helpe me.

notes.label: g
notes.text: By this aſſiſtance of grace, the ſoule continueth in ſpiritual life, and praiſeth God.

verses.text: <na>(h)</na> I haue ſtrayed, as a sheepe, that is loſt: <na>(i)</na> ſeeke thy ſeruant, <na>(k)</na> becauſe I haue not forgotten thy commandmentes.

notes.label: h
notes.text: Al mankind, and vniuerſally euerie one hath bene as a loſt sheepe,

notes.label: i
notes.text: and Chriſt came into this world to ſeeke and ſaue al :

notes.label: k
notes.text: but effectually findeth and ſaueth thoſe only, that forgete not to kepe his commandments.

chapters.summary: A perpetual recommendation of the ſingular excellencie, abſolute neceſſitie, and eternal heauenlie profite of Gods law : with frequent aſpirations to perfection, hatred of ſinne, loue of vertue, and feruent deſire to reſt in God. <na>[1]</na>

summary_notes.text:
Perfect juſtice is in keeping God's law.
The 7. key.

articles.title: GENERAL ANNOTATIONS UPON THIS CXVIII. PSALM.
articles.text:
As this Psalm is the longest in the whole Psalter, so it seemeth to the ancient Fathers most profound in sense. And so much the harder to be understood, because also the very hardness <mn>[1]</mn> thereof lieth hidden, which in diverse other Psalms and parts of holy Scripture, easily appeareth to the reader. But here the words being clear, and the sense also plain and easy in some points of doctrine, yet the more diligence is employed, the more difficulty is found in searching the whole sense and meaning of every word and sentence, with the manner observed in composing it, and the frequent repetition of the same or like words. All which maturely considered caused that great Clerk, and light of the Church Saint Augustin, to omit this Psalm, when he explicated all the <mn>[2]</mn> rest. And when at last he added also this, he wittingly omitted one special difficulty, which he doubted not to be contained in the manner of composing it, not only by order of the Hebrew Alphabet, as diverse more Psalms, and some other parts of holy Scripture, but more artificially than any other, the first eight verses all beginning with the first letter Aleph; the next eight, with the second letter Beth: and so to the last of the two and twenty letters. Of which omission he yieldeth this only reason, because he found nothing (as he humbly affirmeth) that might properly pertain thereunto. Confessing also expressly, that whensoever he applied his cogitations to expound the text it-self, it always exceeded his hability. But finally to satisfy the often and earnest request of his brethren and friends, trusting (as always) in God's special help, he largely expoundeth it, in thirty two distinct Sermons. <mn>[3]</mn>

S. Ambrose, also moved with like piety, made two and twenty Sermons in exposition of this <mn>[4]</mn> Psalm. Affirming in his Prologue, that amongst other Psalms, especially this sheweth how great a master King David was of moral good life. For all Moral doctrine, being of his own nature sweet, yet most delighteth the ears, and gently toucheth the mind, being uttered, as here it is, with pleasantness of verse, and sweetness of song. Again whereas this Royal Prophet in many places of this book poureth out sentences of moral Psalms or songs, as bright stars, that shine and <mn>[5]</mn> glister to all the world, here most excellently he produceth a more singular mirror, as the sun, of full light, burning with meridian heat. And for the profit of all, the better to draw our <mn>[6]</mn> attentions, to learn that we may, though we cannot attain to all that we would, he disposed this Psalm through all the Alphabet: that as children beginning with the first letters, make entrance to further knowledge; so by the same beginnings we should lay the first foundation, and thereupon proceed in our spiritual building, towards perfection in good life, the true service of God. Which is yet further insinuated (as the same Doctor teacheth) by the eight verses continually beginning with the same letter, and so other eight in order through the whole Alphabet, to signify that <mn>[7]</mn> after seven days travail in this temporal life, we may come to that unity, which we expected in the eighth day of resurrection, when we hope to rise revived in our Lord Jesus, in newness of eternal life.

Likewise Saint Basil in the Argument of this Psalm admonisheth, that whereas holy David, <mn>◦</mn> according to diverse states, which he passed, writ diverse Psalms: as when he fled from his enemies, when he lamented his distresses, mourned in pensiveness, enjoyed peace and comfort, ran a right course of virtue, fell from God by sin, & again returning observed God's laws; in this one Psalm he comprehendeth all his prayers made to God at sundry times, & here proposeth the same, a certain profitable moral doctrine, to all sorts and states of men. Neither doth he pretermit doctrinal points of faith, but interposeth them also with moral documents, in such sort, that this one Psalm may suffice to teach the well disposed, how to attain to perfection in virtue, to stir up the slothful unto diligent care of their souls, to recreate the desolate with spiritual consolations, & briefly it administereth all kind of medicine to the diverse passions of mortal men.

For the like judgements of other Fathers we remit the learned reader, to Saint Hilary, <mn>[8]</mn> Theodoret, Prosper, Arnobius, Cassiodorus, Beda, Euthymius, and others, but cannot well omit a brief instruction of S. Jerome. Who in his Epistle to Paula Urbica: not only sheweth the interpretation of the two and twenty letters, but also explicateth their sense in this place, by connecting them into certain short sentences, in this manner: <mn>[9]</mn>



Which is the first connection, signifying that the doctrine of the house, that is the Church of God, is found in the fullness of divine books.
The second connection is:



For what other life can there be without knowledge of Scriptures? Whereby also Christ is known, who is the life of them that believe in him.
The third connection is: <mn>◦</mn>



Albeit we now could know all things which are written, yet we know but in part, and in part we prophesy: for we see now by a glass, in a dark sort, but when we shall be worthy to be with <mn>[10]</mn> Christ, and shall be like to Angels, then doctrine of books shall cease, & then we shall see face to face the Good Beginning, even as he is. <mn>[11]</mn>

The fourth connection is: <mn>◦</mn>



The hands are understood in work, heart and discipline are understood in sense or meaning, because we cannot rightly do any thing, unless we first know what things are to be done. The fifth connection is:



This needeth not explication, for it is manifest as the light, that from Scriptures are eternal helps. The sixth connection is:



According to that which we have expounded in the fourth connection: that deeds & intention must concur.
The seventh connection which is last, in which number of seven is also mystical understanding:



Distinct voice is produced by the teeth, & in these signs we come to the Head of all which is Christ, by whom we have access to the everlasting Kingdom.
Or thus (not transposing the words) By vocation of Christ the Head, through distinct voice of signs (for words are signs shewing the mind) we are conducted to the eternal Kingdom, the happiness which all men desire.
What I pray thee (saith this holy Doctor) is more sacred than this mystery, what more pleasant than this delight? What meat, & what honey are sweeter, than to know God's wisdom; to enter into his secret closet; to behold the sense of our Creator; and to teach the words of thy Lord God, full of spiritual wisdom, which are derided by the wise of this world.
We must also advertise the reader of the like discourses of ancient Fathers (over long to be here recited) concerning the manifold high praises of God's Law, contained in this Psalm, with <mn>[12]</mn> frequent repetition of certain Synonyma words signifying the same thing, in all fourteen, to wit: The Law of God, his Ways, Testimonies, Commandments, Precepts, Statutes, Justifications, <mn>[13]</mn> Judgements, Justice, Equity, Verity, Words, Speeches, & Sermons: of which there is commonly one, in every verse, & sometimes two or three in the same verse. But our English tongue hardly sufficing rightly, to distinguish the three last, which in Latin are Verba, Eloquia, Sermones, we translate WORDS only, adding in the margin, Eloquia, and Sermones, when they occur.

Leaving therefore larger commentaries to others; we shall prosecute our wonted manner of brief glosses. Only here premonishing the diligent readers, especially Clergyman (ourselves and our brethren) who every day sing or read this whole Psalm in the Canonical hours, to observe two particular points of Christian doctrine, evidently proved by many places of this Psalm. The one against the Pelagians' heresy, denying the necessity of God's special grace in meritorious works. For the Psalmist often here inculcateth man's insufficiency, that of himself, and by natural <mn>[14]</mn> forces, he cannot keep the commandments of God, but needeth always the particular grace of God, as well to believe in him, to repent for sins, and to begin good works; as to proceed, and persevere in good state to the end. The other against the heresy of our time, denying merit by grace & freewill. For here it is also manifest, that God's grace maketh man able, to keep his <mn>[15]</mn> commandments, and by keeping them to become just in this life, and so to merit eternal glory. Sundry other principal Articles of Christian Catholic Religion are likewise comprised in this one Psalm: but especially Moral doctrine.

verses.text: A gradual Canticle. WHEN I was in tribulation I cried to our Lord: and <na>(a)</na> he heard me.

notes.label: a
notes.text: Former experience of Gods mercie in hearing the prayers of thoſe that inuocated him, geueth hope that he wil heare in like caſe.

verses.text: O Lord deliuer my ſoule from <na>(b)</na> vniuſt lippes, and from a deceiptful tongue.

notes.label: b
notes.text: Nothing is more dangerous then vntrue and deceiptful tongues, nothing more damage then to diminish, and detract from the good fame of the iuſt : and therfore this is a moſt neceſſarie prayer, that God wil deliuer vs, from the wicked tongues of Turkes, Heretikes, and other wicked men.

verses.text: <na>(c)</na> What may be geuen thee, or what may be added vnto thee, to a deceiptful tongue?

notes.label: c
notes.text: What punishment is great ynough for wicked tongues?

verses.text: <na>(d)</na> The sharpe arrowes of the mightie, with coales of deſolation.

notes.label: d
notes.text: Surely the malice of wicked tongues deſerueth sharpeſt punishments to be afflicted by ſtrong handes.

verses.text: <na>(e)</na> Woe is to me, that my ſeiourning is prolonged: I haue dwelte with the <na>(f)</na> inhabitantes of Cedar:

notes.label: e
notes.text: Iewes lamented their long abſence from the holie land, eſpecially from Ieruſalem, and the Temple. Chriſtians mourne for their reſtraint from Gods Seruice, and long perigrination from heauen.

notes.label: f
notes.text: Of Cedar the ſonne of Iſmael, came Mahomet, the Turkes falſe prophet, whoſe tyrannie is great and long. The name Cedar is interpreted, blackenes, and obſcuritie, which ſignifieth darkenes of error, and ſinne.

verses.text: My ſoule hath bene long a ſeiourner.
With them, that hated peace, I was peaceable: when I ſpake to them, they impugned me <na>(g)</na> without cauſe.

notes.label: g
notes.text: The wicked afflict thoſe that geue no cauſe of offence.

chapters.summary: The Iewes in captiuitie of Babylon, Chriſtians in perſecution, or other great tribulation, pray with confidence to be deliuered from danger, and ſlander of wicked tongues, 5. lamenting their long indurance. <na>[1]</na>

articles.title: A BRIEF NOTE CONCERNING the Gradual Psalms.
articles.text: Here follow in order fifteen Psalms entitle Gradual Canticles. The Hebrew word Mahaloth <mn>[1]</mn> signifieth Steps, or Ascensions. The reason whereof Aadias, and some other Rabbins yield, for that they were sung with highest elevated notes, that can be in Music. The Talmud saith they are so called, because they were sung in the fifteen steps going up into the Temple. But S. Augustin, S. Basil, and other Christian Fathers expound them according to the history, and immediate prophetical sense, of the delivery of the Jews from captivity of Babylon, ascending into <mn>[2]</mn> Jerusalem: which is so situated on mountains, that the way from all parts was by ascending unto it. According to the Mystical sense, of ascending spiritually by virtues to perfection, and to <mn>[3]</mn> eternal felicity. For the way tending to virtue (saith S. Basil) is like to certain steps (or degrees) by little and little bringing the man that loveth wisdom unto heaven. These Canticles therefore are prayers, mixed with consolations, for the joyful delivery of God's people, from that great captivity in Babylon, which the Psalmist King David saw in prophetical spirit, and which his posterity felt, and sometime endured. Which again as a figure signifieth the return and ascending of mankind from sin to grace, and from the miserable state of this world into heaven. Whereupon S. Augustine interpreteth this prophecy of the ascension, or elevation of the heart, from the vale of tears. In <mn>[4]</mn> the mean time, whiles we are in this world, these Psalms are consolatory prayers, and prophetical assurance, that God's people, Catholic Christians, shall be delivered from the thraldom and persecution of Pagans, Turks, and Heretics. As partly we see by the delivery from the Roman persecuting Emperors, from the Vandals, Goths, and Huns: & therefore with assured confidence we hope and expect the like delivery from Turks, and all Heretics of Luther's brood.

The historical sense.
The mystical sense.
These Psalms are consolatory prayers and prophecies.

summary_notes.text:
Prayer in tribulation.
The 7. key.

verses.text: A gradual Canticle. I HAVE lifted vp mine eies vnto <na>(a)</na> the mountaines, <na>(b)</na> from whence helpe shal come to me.

notes.label: a
notes.text: Towardes Ieruſalem, and towards heauen.

notes.label: b
notes.text: Al helpe cometh from heauen, that is, from God, who of his diuine ordinance eſpecially heareth prayers made in holie places. 3. Reg. 7.

verses.text: My helpe is from our Lord, who made heauen and earth.
Geue he not <na>(c)</na> thy foote to be moued: neither doe he ſlumber that keepeth thee.

notes.label: c
notes.text: The iuſt ſpeaketh and wisheth wel to his owne ſoule. Eſpecially the whole Church reioyceth in Gods aſſured protection.

verses.text: Loe he shal not ſlumber nor ſleepe, that kepeth <na>(d)</na> Iſrael.

notes.label: d
notes.text: The militant Church.

verses.text: Our lord kepeth thee, our Lord is thy protection, vpon thy right hand.
By day <na>(e)</na> the ſunne shal not burne thee: nor <na>(f)</na> the moone by night.

notes.label: e
notes.text: Proſperitie,

notes.label: f
notes.text: nor aduerſitie can ouerthrow the Church.

verses.text: Our Lord doth kepe thee from al euil: our Lord kepe <na>(g)</na> thy ſoule.

notes.label: g
notes.text: ſpiritual life.

verses.text: Our Lord kepe thy coming in, and thy going out: from hence forth now, and for euer.

chapters.summary: The iuſt reioyce that their prayer is heard, and that God continually protecteth them. <na>[1]</na>

summary_notes.text:
God's protection.
The 3. key.

verses.text: A gradual Canticle. I REIOYCED in theſe thinges, which <na>(a)</na> were ſayd to me: We shal goe into the houſe of our Lord.

notes.label: a
notes.text: Diuers Prophetes told the Iewes in captiuitie, that they ſhould returne to Ieruſalem. Al Prophetes, Chriſt alſo, and his Apoſtles, and Prieſtes preach the entrance, and ioyes of heauen to the iuſt. Al vvhich the Pſalmiſt ſaw in propheticall ſpirite, and reioyced.

verses.text: <na>(b)</na> Our feete were ſtanding, in thy courtes ô Ieruſalem

notes.label: b
notes.text: The Iewes conſider that ſometimes they vvere ioyful in the Temple of Ieruſalem : Chriſtians reioyce in the comforte they haue in the militant Church.

verses.text: Ieruſalem, which is built as a citie: whoſe <na>(c)</na> participation is together in it ſelf.

notes.label: c
notes.text: Communitie and participation of ſpirituall graces, is a great ioy to Catholiques, wherof the ſame Prophet ſpeaketh, Pſal 118. v. 6, and often els where.

verses.text: For <na>(d)</na> thither did the tribes aſcend, <na>(e)</na> the tribes of our Lord: the teſtimonie of Iſrael to confeſſe vnto the name of our Lord.

notes.label: d
notes.text: Al the twelue Tribes frequented Ieruſalem,

notes.label: e
notes.text: and al nations of the world do come to the Catholique Church.

verses.text: Becauſe ſeates <na>(f)</na> ſate there in iudgement, <na>(g)</na> ſeates vpon the houſe <na>(h)</na> of Dauid.

notes.label: f
notes.text: Seates of Iudgement vvere placed in Ieruſalem,

notes.label: g
notes.text: and ſeates of Iudgement in the Catholique Church

notes.label: h
notes.text: of Chriſt.

verses.text: <na>(i)</na> Aske ye the thinges that are for the peace of Ieruſalem: and <na>(k)</na> abundance to them that loue thee.

notes.label: i
notes.text: Chriſt exhorteth to aske,

notes.label: k
notes.text: and promiſeth to geue that is rightly asked ; Chriſtians alſo inuite each other to pray for the Church.

verses.text: Peace be made in thy ſtrength: and abundance in thy towers.
<na>(l)</na> For my bretheren, and my neigbours ſakes, <na>(m)</na> I ſpake peace of thee:

notes.label: l
notes.text: Chriſt prayeth for his Church,

notes.label: m
notes.text: and gaue his peace to the Apoſtles, and in them to their ſucceſſors.

verses.text: For the houſe of our Lord God, I haue ſought <na>(n)</na> good thinges to thee.

notes.label: n
notes.text: For in heauenlie Ieruſalem, al good thinges are prepared, & are geuen to Sainctes reigning there for euer.

chapters.summary: Vnder the figure of returne to Ieruſalem, vehemently deſired by the Iewes in captiuitie, the Pſalmiſt deſcribeth the deſire, and hope of the iuſt to poſſeſſe heauen. <na>[1]</na>

summary_notes.text:
Ioyes of heauen promiſed to the iuſt.
The 10. key.

verses.text: A gradual Canticle. TO thee haue I lifted vp mine eies, which dwelleſt in the heauens.

Behold as the eies <na>(a)</na> of ſeruantes, are on the handes of their maſters, As the eies <na>(b)</na> of the handmaide on the handes of her miſtreſſe: ſo are our eies to our Lord God vntil he haue mercie on vs.

notes.label: a
notes.text: Seruantes expecting neceſſaries at their maſters handes, are commonly very attentiue to receiue that vvhich they hope for : ſo muſt the faithful praying God, be very attentiue, and not diſtracted in their prayers.

notes.label: b
notes.text: An other example of handmaides, who generally are more diligent then men.

verses.text: Haue mercie on vs ô Lord, haue mercie on vs: becauſe we are <na>(c)</na> much replenished with contempt.

notes.label: c
notes.text: Though God ſuffer his ſeruantes to ſuſtaine ſome affliction and reproch, yet he heareth and deliuereth them before they be oppreſſed.

verses.text: Becauſe our ſoule is <na>(d)</na> much replenished: reproch to them that abund, and contempt to the prowde.

notes.label: d
notes.text: Seing perſecution ſtil increaſe, or continew long, the faithful are then ſpecially to conceiue hope of ſpeedie reliefe.

chapters.summary: A feruent and attentiue prayer, to be deliuered from captiuitie, or anie other affliction. <na>[1]</na>

summary_notes.text:
A prayer in affliction.
The 7. key.

verses.text: A gradual Canticle. BVt that our Lord <na>(a)</na> was in vs, let Iſrael now ſay:

notes.label: a
notes.text: If God had not ſent his helpe, and defence to vs,

verses.text: but that our Lord was in vs, <na>(b)</na> When men roſe vp againſt vs,

notes.label: b
notes.text: we could not haue eſcaped the force of our enimies.

verses.text: <na>(c)</na> perhaps they had ſwalowed vs <na>(d)</na> aliue: When their furie was angrie againſt vs,

notes.label: c
notes.text: The word [perhaps] doth not here import a doubt, or vncertaintie, but in modeſt maner of aſſeueration, leaueth the iudgement of the euent that should hapen (if God did not protect his ſeruantes) to their ovvne conſideration : which is an vſual phraſe in moſt langnages.

notes.label: d
notes.text: So ſudainly ſhould the weake, without Gods protection, be deſtroyed, as men are deuoured & ſwalowed vp by rauening wild beaſtes, euen before they be throughly dead. So vvas Ionas ſwalowed into the vvhales bellie.

verses.text: perhaps <na>(e)</na> water had ſwalowed vs.

notes.label: e
notes.text: Furious perſecution.

verses.text: Our ſoule hath paſſed through <na>(f)</na> a torrent: perhaps our ſoule had paſſed through an intolerable water.

notes.label: f
notes.text: Suddaine great trubles.

verses.text: Bleſſed be our Lord which hath not geuen vs, for a pray to their teeth.
Our ſoule as a ſparow is deliuered from the ſnare of the fowlers: The ſnare is <na>(g)</na> broken, and we are deliuered.

notes.label: g
notes.text: Mans ſubtelue often deceiueth an other man, but there is no counſel able to circumuent God.

verses.text: Our helpe is in the name of our Lord, who made heauen and earth.

chapters.summary: The whole Church, and euerie iuſt perſon, gratfully confeſſeth, that by Gods protection they are ſecure, without which none could eſcape ruine. <na>[1]</na>

summary_notes.text:
Gods protection.
The 3. key.

verses.text: A gradual Canticle. THEY <na>(a)</na> that truſt in our Lord, as mount Sion: he shal not be moued for euer, <na>(b)</na> that dwelleth in Ieruſalem.

notes.label: a
notes.text: Thoſe that confidently truſt in God, are in ſuch ſecuritie as is mount Sion, which is a hil, defended alſo with other hilles round about.

notes.label: b
notes.text: An other thing required to this ſecuritie, is to dwel vvithin Ieruſalem, not the terreſtrial citie, for (as S. Auguſtin obſerueth) the Ievves that dwelt therin are deſtroyed or made captiues, and hitherto reiected of God, but in the Catholique Church.

verses.text: Mountaines round about it: and our Lord round about his people, from hence forth now and for euer.
Becauſe our Lord <na>(c)</na> wil not leaue the rod of ſinners vpon the lote of the iuſt: that the iuſt reach not their handes to iniquitie.

notes.label: c
notes.text: God wil not alwayes, nor finally leaue his ſeruants in tribulation, but only a while for their good.

verses.text: <na>(d)</na> Doe wel ô Lord to the good, and right of hart.

notes.label: d
notes.text: This prayer is alſo an aſſeueration, for it is certaine that God wil defend, and reward the good, and right of hart:

verses.text: But <na>(e)</na> thoſe that decline into obligations, our Lord wil bring with them that worke iniquitie: <na>(f)</na> peace vpon Iſrael.

notes.label: e
notes.text: And no leſſe aſſuredly God wil punish not only the notorious wicked, and principal auctors of wickednes, but alſo al thoſe that for feare or for commoditie, or for anie other cauſe, decline into obligations, bondes, couenants, or anie way conſent, in external shew with the wicked againſt God, as in outward profeſſion of Hereſie, or Schiſme, though ſuch temporizers do not thinke in their hart, that the pretended religion is true, wherto they are drawe to yeld external conformitie. For, as the Pſalmiſt here teacheth, our Lord wil bring al ſuch acceſſarie offenders, to the ſame iudgement and puniſhment, vvith the principal vvorkers of iniquitie.

notes.label: f
notes.text: Al vvhich being puniſhed, then Ieruſalem, the Catholique Church, shal haue peace.

chapters.summary: The Church, and holie members therof, are alwayes protected by God: 5. The wicked being ſuffered for a while, are at laſt punished. <na>[1]</na>

summary_notes.text:
God's protection.
The 3. key.

verses.text: A gradual Canticle. WHEN our Lord turned the captiuitie of Sion: we were made as <na>(a)</na> men comforted.

notes.label: a
notes.text: The Ievves releaſed from captiuitie, vvere exceedingly, and almoſt incredibly comforted, as men for great, and vnexpected ſundaine ioy thinke it rather a dreame, then a truth that they are deliuered from miſeries. So S. Peter when he vvas deliuered out of priſon by an Angel. Act. 12. thought it rather a viſion, then a true deliuerie. Such ſpiritual ioy deuoute ſoules haue vvhen they are deliuered from ſinne.

verses.text: Then was our mouth replenished with ioy: and our tongue with exultation. Then <na>(b)</na> shal they ſay among the Gentiles: Our Lord hath done magnifically vvith them.

notes.label: b
notes.text: VVheras in the tvvo former verſes (and very commonly) the Prophet ſpeaketh in the preter tenſe, for the aſſurance of that he foresheweth, as if it vvere already donne, yet here he vttereth his prophecie in the future tenſe, that the Gentiles wil confeſſe that God dealeth magnifically vvith his people.

verses.text: <na>(c)</na> Our Lord hath done magnifically with vs: we are made ioyful.

notes.label: c
notes.text: The people alſo themſelues gratfully confeſſe that God dealeth magnifically with them.

verses.text: <na>(d)</na> Turne our captiuitie ô Lord, <na>(e)</na> as a torrent in the South.

notes.label: d
notes.text: The Prophet forſeing al this in ſpirit, prayeth for the performance hereof.

notes.label: e
notes.text: And that it may ſpedely be done, as a torrent that runneth in the ſouth part of the world. is commonly very great, much deſired, but ſcarſe expected.

verses.text: <na>(f)</na> They that ſow in teares, <na>(g)</na> shal reape in ioyfulneſſe.

notes.label: f
notes.text: This is the ordinarie diſpoſition of God, that his ſeruants shal make their ſeeding, vvhich is, doe good vvorkes (ſaith S. Auguſtin) vvith teares, in tribulation vpon earth:

notes.label: g
notes.text: and reape a plentiful harueſt, the revvard of their ſuffering and vvel vvorking, in the next life. In aſſured hope vvherof the Pſalmiſt, and the vvhole Church ioyfully conclude this Pſalme with the tvvo verſes folovving.

verses.text: Going they went and wept, caſting their ſeedes.
But coming they shal come with exultation, carying their sheaues.

chapters.summary: Iſralites releaſed from captiuitie of Babylon, much more the bleſſed both of the old and new teſtament deliuered by Chriſt from captiuitie of ſinne, do reioyce: 5. Who neuertheles muſt paſſe through tribulation to eternal felicitie. <na>[1]</na>

summary_notes.text:
The deliuered from captiuitie reioyce.
The 7. key.

verses.text: A gradual Canticle <na>(a)</na> of Salomon: VNLESSE <na>(b)</na> our Lord build the houſe, they haue laboured in vayne that build it. Vnleſſe our Lord kepe the citie, he watcheth in vayne that kepeth it.

notes.label: a
notes.text: God not permitting Dauid to build the Temple, promiſed that his ſonne ſhould build it, and therfore beſides other good admonitions, geuen to his ſonne Salomon, he directeth this Pſalme to him, to be ſongue with others in the dedication of the Temple. 3. Reg. 8. 1. Par. 5.

notes.label: b
notes.text: Vnleſſe God be the principal Agent, no worke can proſper.

verses.text: It is vaine for you to riſe <na>(c)</na> before light: <na>(d)</na> riſe ye after ye haue ſitten, which eate <na>(e)</na> the bread of ſorow.

notes.label: c
notes.text: It is vaine to atempt anie thing without Gods grace aſſiſting:

notes.label: d
notes.text: they that ſo doing, & thincking they haue done ſomething, reſt

notes.label: e
notes.text: after their painful trauel, muſt riſe againe & beginne anew, because that which they ſeme to haue done wel, is nothing worth, nor ſhal haue reward.

verses.text: <na>(f)</na> When he shal giue <na>(g)</na> ſleepe to his beloued: behold <na>(h)</na> the inheritance of our Lord <na>(i)</na> are children: <na>(k)</na> the reward, the fruite of the wombe.

notes.label: f
notes.text: Contrariwiſe vvhere God geuing grace, thoſe that truly loue him, do good vvorkes,

notes.label: g
notes.text: with great eaſe, and dilight, as they take their ſleepe,

notes.label: h
notes.text: they merite inheritance in heauen,

notes.label: i
notes.text: for their good vvorkes.

notes.label: k
notes.text: the revvard is promiſed to the true children of God, borne to him in the wombe of the Catholique Church.

verses.text: As <na>(l)</na> arrowes in the hand of the mightie: ſo are the <na>(m)</na> children of them that are shaken.

notes.label: l
notes.text: Moreouer as a ſtrong archer ſtriketh deepe with his arrowes; ſo they that patiently ſuffer much in this world,

notes.label: m
notes.text: do multiplie good workes.

verses.text: <na>(n)</na> Bleſſed is the man that hath filled his deſire of them: he shal <na>(o)</na> not be confounded when he shal ſpeake to his enemies <na>(p)</na> in the gate.

notes.label: n
notes.text: Such shal be very happie,

notes.label: o
notes.text: & very eaſily anſvver al that can be obiected againſt them

notes.label: p
notes.text: in the day of Iudgement.

chapters.summary: Neither houſe nor citie can be built, or kept without Gods ſpecial prouidence and helpe, 3. thoſe that truſt in him shal proſper in their endeuours. <na>[1]</na>

summary_notes.text:
God's help in all good works.
The 3. key.

verses.text: A gradual Canticle. BLESSED are al that feare our Lord, that walke in his wayes.
Becauſe thou shalt eate the labours of thy handes: bleſſed art thou, and it shal be wel with thee.
Thy <na>(a)</na> wife as a fruitful vine, in <na>(b)</na> the ſides of thy houſe. <na>(c)</na> Thy children as young plantes of oliuetrees, round about thy table.

notes.label: a
notes.text: If ſuch ſeruants of God be maried, they shal ordinarily haue iſſue, and ſucceſſion in their familie: but eſpecially the ſoules of ſuch ſhal bring forth manie meritorious workes,

notes.label: b
notes.text: in the boſome of the Catholique Church, vvhich vvas founded in Chriſts ſide.

notes.label: c
notes.text: Children alſo ſignifie good workes.

verses.text: Behold ſo shal the man be bleſſed, that feareth our Lord.
Our Lord out of Sion bleſſe thee: and that thou mayſt ſee the good thinges of Ieruſalem al the dayes of thy life.
And that thou mayſt ſee thy <na>(d)</na> childrens children, peace vpon Iſrael.

notes.label: d
notes.text: Reward in heauen for good workes in earth.

chapters.summary: Happines both of this life and of the next, is obtayned by fearing, and ſincerely ſeruing God. <na>[1]</na>

summary_notes.text:
Feare of God the way to happines.
The 7. key.

verses.text: A gradual Canticle. <na>(a)</na> OFTEN haue they impugned me <na>(b)</na> from my youth, let Iſrael now ſay:

notes.label: a
notes.text: Iſrael which is the Church of God, reioycing ſaith: that enimies haue often,

notes.label: b
notes.text: euen from the beginning of the world, perſecuted me, as when Cain perſecuted Abel, other wicked perſecuted Seth, Enoch, Noe: the Chaldeis perſecuted Abraham: the Ægyptians perſecuted the Iſraelites: and ſo in other generations.

verses.text: Often haue they impugned me from my youth: <na>(c)</na> but they haue not preuailed againſt me.

notes.label: c
notes.text: But they haue neuer ouercome me. So the Pſalmiſt teſtifieth for al times paſt, & prophecieth the ſame for times to come.

verses.text: Sinners <na>(d)</na> haue builded vpon my backe: they haue <na>(e)</na> prolonged their iniquitie.

notes.label: d
notes.text: Perſecuters not being able to ouerthrow, or ſuppreſſe the Church, haue laide great weightie burdens of tribulations vpon her backe, which ſhe hath patiently and ſtrongly borne,

notes.label: e
notes.text: they haue ſtil perſiſted, one ſorte after an other, but with longanimitie the Church hath ſtood faſt, and conſtantly paſſed through al diſtreſſes. In moral ſenſe ſinners build iniquitie vpon the back of the Church, yea and vpon Gods back, when they preſume to ſinne, truſting in the end to be abſolued by vertue of holie Sacraments leift in the Church. Likewiſe when they excuſe their ſinnes, imputing the cauſe to other creatures of God, vvherby they are allured. vvhich is in effect ( ſaith S. Auguſtin) to accuſe God, and to build iniquities on Gods back, vvho made thoſe creatures.

verses.text: <na>(f)</na> Our iuſt Lord wil cut the neckes of ſinners:

notes.label: f
notes.text: God therfore who is iuſt, vvil at laſt caſt ſuch preſumptuous ſinners from his back, and breake their ſtiffe neckes:

verses.text: let them al <na>(g)</na> be confounded and <na>(h)</na> turned backward, that hate Sion.

notes.label: g
notes.text: then shal they be confounded,

notes.label: h
notes.text: ſeparated eternally from God, become like fruitles, and vvithered graſſe, caſt avvay, deſpiſed, yea curſed of al, and bleſſed by none, as the Prophet denounceth in the next verſes.

verses.text: Let them be made as graſſe in the toppes of houſes: which is withered before it be plucked vp.
Wherof the reaper hath not filled his hand, and he that gathereth the sheaues his boſome.
And they ſayd not that paſſed by: The bleſſing of our Lord be vpon you: we haue bleſſed you in the name of our Lord.

chapters.summary: The Church often (3. and much) impugned, is not ouercome. 4. Her perſecuters are deſtroyed, 6. contemned, 8. and curſed. <na>[1]</na>

summary_notes.text:
The Church ſtill firm in perſecution.
The 6. key.

verses.text: A gradual Canticle. FROM <na>(a)</na> the depthes I haue cried to thee ô Lord:

notes.label: a
notes.text: This prayer agreeth to al true penitents, crying to God for helpe, being either in depth of ſorovv for ſinne, and ſo it is one of the Penitential Pſalmes. or the depth of feruent deſire to aſcend tovvards perfection in vertue, and from this vaile of miſerie into heauen. and ſo it is a Gradual Pſalme. or in the depth of temporal paines, and ſo it is a ſpecial prayer for ſoules in Purgatorie, offered by the Church in their behalfe.

verses.text: Lord heare my voice: Let thine eares be intent, to the voice of my petition.
If thou shalt obſerue iniquities ô Lord: Lord <na>(b)</na> who shal ſuſteyne it?

notes.label: b
notes.text: None iſ able to abide the rigour of Gods iuſtice.

verses.text: Becauſe with thee there is <na>(c)</na> propiciation: and for <na>(d)</na> thy law I haue expected thee ô Lord. My ſoule hath expected in his word:

notes.label: c
notes.text: But al muſt relie vpon his mercie.

notes.label: d
notes.text: For thy promiſes made in the law, that thou wilt remitte ſinnes to the penitent, geue more grace to them that ſeeke it, and mitigate alſo the paines due for ſinnes.

verses.text: my ſoule hath hoped in our Lord.
From <na>(e)</na> the morning watch euen vntil night: let Iſrael hope in our Lord.

notes.label: e
notes.text: The hope of penitents is like to the watches of the day time, from morning vntil night, which are more comfortable, then watches of the night:

verses.text: Becauſe with our Lord there is mercie: and with him <na>(f)</na> plenteous redemption.

notes.label: f
notes.text: The greateſt comforth is in Chriſt our Redemer, vvhoſe plentiful Redemption bringeth more abundance of grace.

verses.text: And he shal redeme <na>(g)</na> Iſrael, from al his iniquities.

notes.label: g
notes.text: Chriſts Redemption being ſufficient for al the vvorld, is effectual only to true liuing members of the Catholique Church.

chapters.summary: The Iewes, or other people in tribulation for ſinne, or temporal captiuitie, crie to God to be deliuered: 4. truſting, and encoreging ech other in Gods accuſtomed mercie, aſſuredly hoping that he wil redeme & deliuer them. <na>[1]</na>

summary_notes.text:
The ſixth penitential Pſalm.
The 7. key.

verses.text: A gradual Canticle of <na>(a)</na> Dauid. LORD my hart is not exalted: <na>(b)</na> neither are mine eies loftie. Neither haue I walked in great matters: nor in meruelous thinges aboue me.

notes.label: a
notes.text: Dauid by Gods ſpecial grace hauing a ſincere minde tovvards al men, euen towards his enimies, and an humble hart, not deſiring anie thing ambiciouſly, but al to the honour of God, propoſeth his owne example, for others to imitate: that they may vvith him offer the ſacrifice of humilitie, and innocencie vnto God, from whom al good thinges procede.

notes.label: b
notes.text: Al this vvith a thankful mind to God vvho gaue this grace.

verses.text: If I was not humbly mynded: but exalted my ſoule: As <na>(c)</na> the weaned childe is toward his mother, <na>(d)</na> ſo retribution in my ſoule.

notes.label: c
notes.text: As children after they are vveaned come ſtil vvillingly to their mother, ſo doth the childe of God relie vpon Gods helpe, though he alwayes feele not the ſame ſwetnes:

notes.label: d
notes.text: & according to his demeanur herein, he expecteth reward.

verses.text: <na>(e)</na> Let Iſrael hope in our Lord, from henceforth now and for euer.

notes.label: e
notes.text: King Dauid, or anie other being for his vertue aduanced, and revvarded by God, is a good example to moue others to do the like, ſo shal they receiue like reward.

chapters.summary: Anie iuſt ſoule in humble confidence offereth his innocencie, as a ſpiritual and gratful ſacrifice to God, 3. exhorting al Gods ſeruants euer to hope in him. <na>[1]</na>

summary_notes.text:
Confidence of innocencie.
The 7. key.

verses.text: A gradual Canticle. REMEMBER <na>(a)</na> Dauid ô Lord, and al his meekenes:

notes.label: a
notes.text: It is an vſual thing that Dauid, Moyſes, & other Prophetes ſpeake of themſelues in the third perſon.

verses.text: As he ſware to our Lord, <na>(b)</na> vowed a vowe to the God of Iacob.

notes.label: b
notes.text: King Dauid deſiring, and ſo farre as lay in him, promiſing to build a Temple to God, vvith great inſtance prayed that he might performe the ſame. But God diſpoſing othervviſe, that not he, but his ſonne ſhould build it, he neuertheles prepared the matter, workemen, and money, ſhevved the forme, and diſpoſed the Leuites how to ſerue therin.

verses.text: <na>(c)</na> If I shal enter into the tabernacle of my houſe, if I shal aſcend into the bed of my couch.

notes.label: c
notes.text: Moreouer by vow depriued himſelf of entering into his owne houſe, or taking his ordinarie reſt, til he might (if it ſo pleaſed God) know the place where it ſhould be built.

verses.text: If I shal geue ſleepe to mine eies, and ſlumbering to mine eie liddes:
And reſt to my temples: vntil I finde a place for our Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Iacob.
Behold we haue heard of it <na>(d)</na> in Ephrata: we haue found it in <na>(e)</na> the fildes of the wood.

notes.label: d
notes.text: It vvas reueled to Dauid, that the Temple ſhould be built, in that part of Ieruſalem, vvhich looketh tovvards Bethleem (othervviſe called Ephrata) vvhere our Sauiour vvas borne.

notes.label: e
notes.text: VVithin Ieruſalem, which is compaſſed with vvoodes. In this viſion alſo the whole forme of the Temple vvas reueled vnto him, as he teſtifieth. 1. Par. 28. v. 19. Al thinges, quoth he, came vvritten with the hand of our Lord vnto me: that I might vnderſtand al the vvorkes of the paterne.

verses.text: <na>(f)</na> We wil enter into his tabernacle: we wil <na>(g)</na> adore in the place where his feete ſtood.

notes.label: f
notes.text: Holie Dauid moued vvith exceding deuotion, repared to the place, vvhere Gods Temple should be built:

notes.label: g
notes.text: & adored God, vvhere the Propitiatorie, as a footſtoole repreſenting Gods preſence, ſhould ſtand. What meruel then if deuotion moue Chriſtians, to viſite the holie places, vvhere our Sauiour, God and Man was Incarnate, vvas borne, ſuffered death, vvas buried, aſcended into heauen, or anie other place where his feete ſtood.

verses.text: <na>(h)</na> Ariſe Lord into thy reſt, thou and <na>(i)</na> the arke of thy ſanctification.

notes.label: h
notes.text: O God, leauing Silo, Gabaon, and the like places, come into thy holie Temple.

notes.label: i
notes.text: With the Arke of conenant, vvhere thou ſanctifieſt thy people. And here againe the Prophet illuminated vvith a higher Myſterie, and inflamed with more deuotion, prayeth for Chriſtes coming into the world, and that after his Paſſion he wil riſe, not only in glorie of ſoule, but alſo of bodie, prefigured by the Arke of teſtimonie, which vvas in the tabernacle, and after in the Temple.

verses.text: Let thy Prieſtes be clothed with <na>(k)</na> iuſtice: & let thy <na>(l)</na> ſainctes reioyce.

notes.label: k
notes.text: Grant therfore that thy Prieſtes, vvhich muſt offer ſacrifice in this ſacred place, be indued with vertues, and good life worthie of their degree:

notes.label: l
notes.text: and the Leuites who are ordained to ſerue there, be likevviſe made fitte for their diuers functions, both in the old and new Teſtament.

verses.text: <na>(m)</na> For Dauid thy ſeruants ſake, <na>(n)</na> turne not away the face of thy Chriſt.

notes.label: m
notes.text: And ſeing thou haſt geuen ſuch meeknes, deuotion, zele, ſinceritie, and other vertues making him a man according to thyne owne hart, and therupon promiſed to eſtablish his ſede,

notes.label: n
notes.text: differ not to ſend thy promiſed Meſſias, Chriſt our Redemer.

verses.text: Our Lord <na>(o)</na> hath ſworne truth to Dauid, and <na>(p)</na> he wil not diſapoint it: <na>(q)</na> Of the fruite of thy wombe I vvil ſet vpon thy ſeate.

notes.label: o
notes.text: Henceforth to the end of this Pſalme, the Prophet relateth Gods reuelation to him: That he hath truly promiſed with an oath,

notes.label: p
notes.text: and vvil performe,

notes.label: q
notes.text: to ſette one of Dauids ſonnes vpon his Throne: which vvas not only fulfilled in Salomon, who reigned in great peace, and builded the Temple, but eſpecially in Chriſt the Sonne of Dauid, to whom our Lord God gaue the ſeate of Dauid his father, & he shal reigne in the houſe of Iacob for euer, and of his kingdom there shal be no end. Luc. 1. v. 32. 33. By this promiſe S. Peter alſo proueth Chriſts Reſurrection. Act. 1. v. 30.

verses.text: <na>(r)</na> If thy children shal keepe my teſtament, and theſe my teſtimonies which I wil teach them: Their children alſo euen for euer, shal ſit vpon thy ſeate.

notes.label: r
notes.text: Concerning the children of Chriſt, members of his kingdom the Church, the promiſe is conditional, if they obſerue Gods commandments, they ſhal ſit vpon his ſeate: be coheyres of his kingdom. Rom. 8. v. 17.

verses.text: Becauſe our Lord hath choſen Sion: he hath choſen it for an habitation to himſelf.
This is my <na>(s)</na> reſt for euer and euer: here wil I dwel becauſe I haue choſen it.

notes.label: s
notes.text: Sion, the Catholique Church, is a perpetual place where God dwelleth.

verses.text: Bleſſing I wil bleſſe her <na>(t)</na> widow: her <na>(v)</na> poore I wil fil with breades.

notes.label: t
notes.text: The Church vvanting Chriſts viſible preſence, is replenished with manie bleſſinges,

notes.label: v
notes.text: and al her humble children are releeued vvith holie Sacraments.

verses.text: Her <na>(w)</na> Prieſtes I wil clothe with ſaluation: and her <na>(x)</na> ſainctes shal reioyce with ioyfulnes.

notes.label: w
notes.text: The Church hath alwayes ſome holie Prieſtes,

notes.label: x
notes.text: and ſome holie people.

verses.text: <na>(y)</na> Thither wil I bring forth a horne to Dauid, I haue prepared <na>(z)</na> a lampe to my Chriſt.

notes.label: y
notes.text: Of this Church, elected by God, Chriſt is the Protector, and ſtrong defence.

notes.label: z
notes.text: and the ſame Church shal be a perpetual lampe, wherby others may come to him.

verses.text: His enemies I wil clothe with confuſion: but vpon him shal my ſanctification florish.

chapters.summary: The Pſalmiſt earneſtly prayeth God to geue him leaue, & to shew him where, to build a Temple. But more eſpecially prayeth for, and prophecieth the coming of Chriſt, the promiſed Sonne of Dauid, 14. ſignifying Gods promiſe therof, and of eſtablishing his Church. <na>[1]</na>

summary_notes.text:
Chriſt's coming to reſtore man.
The 5. key.

verses.text: A gradual Canticle <na>(a)</na> of Dauid. BEHOLD <na>(b)</na> how good, and how pleaſant a thing it is, for brethren to dwel in one:

notes.label: a
notes.text: Dauid being a moſt peaceable man, euen tovvard his enimies, is added by Eſdras in this title, as an example for others to imitate.

notes.label: b
notes.text: That concord is both good and pleaſant, nedeth no other proofe, but only to conſider, & to behold the fruict therof in euerie communitie, and eſpecially in the Church of God.

verses.text: <na>(c)</na> As oyntement on <na>(d)</na> the head, which ranne downe vpon the beard, <na>(e)</na> the beard of Aaron, which ranne downe vnto <na>(f)</na> the hemme of his garment:

notes.label: c
notes.text: The ointment, wherwith Aaron, and other High Prieſtes vvere conſecrated, was precious, and moſt odoriferous, ſignifying grace bought by Chriſts blood, and producing vertues, vvhich make ſvvete ſauoure:

notes.label: d
notes.text: vvas povvred vpon the High Prieſts head, who being head of the Church,

notes.label: e
notes.text: vnitie and concord deſcended from him to other Prieſtes,

notes.label: f
notes.text: and ſo to the people, euen to the lovveſt, and meaneſt in Gods Church.

verses.text: <na>(g)</na> As the dew of Hermon, which runneth downe vpon mount Sion. Becauſe <na>(h)</na> there hath our Lord commanded bleſſing, and life euen for euer.

notes.label: g
notes.text: An other ſimilitude to declare the excellencie of concord: As the dew of mount Hermon, vvhich is perpetually couered vvith ſnow, that falleth from the heauen, thence deſcending refresheth & fructifieth the hil of Sion: ſo mutual concord, and fraternal charitie amongſt the faithful, nourisheth each other, making them fructful in al good workes.

notes.label: h
notes.text: VVhere there is vnitie God geueth abundance of grace, as where the Apoſtles vvith other faithful vvere geathered, and continued in prayer, the Holie Ghoſt came vpon them al. And the multitude of beleuers [then increaſing] had one hart and one ſoule. Act. 2. &. 4. v. 32.

chapters.summary: Fraternal concord is commended to al in the Church, as neceſſarie and delectable in it ſelf, and bleſſed of God. <na>[1]</na>

summary_notes.text:
Fraternal concord.
The 7. key.

verses.text: A gradual Canticle. LOE <na>(a)</na> now bleſſe our Lord, al ye the ſeruantes of our Lord: which ſtand in the houſe of our Lord, in the courtes of the houſe of our God.

notes.label: a
notes.text: This laſt Gradual Pſalme, as a concluſion exhorteth al to praiſe God:

verses.text: In the nightes lift vp your handes vnto the holie places, and bleſſe ye our Lord.
Our Lord out of Sion bleſſe thee, who <na>(b)</na> made heauen and earth.

notes.label: b
notes.text: for to this end he made al creatures in heauen & in earth.

chapters.summary: Al, and eſpecially clergie men that ſerue the Church, are inuited to prayſe God by day and by night, ſo shal they be bleſſed of God. <na>[1]</na>

summary_notes.text:
God continually to be praiſed.
The 1. key.

verses.text: Allelu ia. PRAYSE ye the name of our Lord, <na>(a)</na> ye ſeruantes prayſe our Lord.

notes.label: a
notes.text: Gods ſeruantes.

verses.text: Ye <na>(b)</na> that ſtand in the houſe of our Lord, in <na>(c)</na> the courtes of the houſe of our God.

notes.label: b
notes.text: Clergie that ſerue in the Temple,

notes.label: c
notes.text: and ye Leuite that attend to his ſeruice, muſt praiſe him for theſe cauſes.

verses.text: Prayſe ye our Lord, becauſe our Lord is <na>(d)</na> good: ſing ye to his name, becauſe it is <na>(e)</na> ſweete.

notes.label: d
notes.text: his goodnes.

notes.label: e
notes.text: his benignitie.

verses.text: Becauſe our Lord <na>(f)</na> hath choſen Iacob to himſelf, Iſrael for his owne poſſeſſion.

notes.label: f
notes.text: he hath adopted vs his children.

verses.text: Becauſe I haue knowne that our Lord is <na>(g)</na> great, and our God aboue al goddes.

notes.label: g
notes.text: he is omnipotent, as appeareth by his workes, here and elſvvhere recited : and manie wayes knovvne to the world.

verses.text: Al thinges whatſoeuer our Lord would he hath done, in heauen, in earth, in the ſea, and in al the depthes.
Bringing forth clowdes from the vttermoſt of the earth: lightenings he hath turned into rayne. Who bringeth forth the windes out of his treaſures:
who ſtroke the firſt begotten of Ægypt from man euen to beaſt.
He ſent forth ſignes, and wonders in the middes of thee ô Ægypt: vpon Pharao, and vpon al his ſeruantes. <cr>[1]</cr>
Who ſtroke manie nations: and ſlew ſtrong kinges:
Sehon the king of the Amorrheites, & Og the king of Baſan, and al the kingdomes of Chanaan. <cr>[1]</cr>
And he gaue their land for inheritance, for an inheritance to Iſrael his people.
Lord thy name is for euer: Lord thy memorial is vnto generation and generation.
Becauſe our Lord shal iudge his people: and wil be intreated toward his ſeruantes.
The idoles of the Gentiles are ſiluer, and gold, the workes of mens handes.
They haue mouth, and shal not ſpeake: they haue eies, and shal not ſee.
They haue eares, and shal not heare: for neither is there breath in their mouth.
Let them that make them become like to them: and al that haue confidence in them.
Ye houſe of Iſrael bleſſe our Lord: ye houſe of Aaron bleſſe our Lord.
Ye houſe of Leui bleſſe our Lord: you that feare our Lord, bleſſe ye our Lord.
Bleſſed be our Lord out of Sion, who dwelleth in Ieruſalem.

chapters.summary: God who only is omnipotent, and fountaine of al goodnes, is of al to be praiſed, 3. He is the ſpecial protector of his elected people. 15. Contrariwiſe falſe goddes are impotent, vaine, and can not helpe thoſe that ſerue them. 19. Only the Church doth rightly praiſe him. <na>[1]</na>

summary_notes.text:
God's perfection and goodneſs.
The 1. key.

verses.text: Allelu ia. CONFESSE ye to our Lord <na>(a)</na> becauſe he is good: <na>(b)</na> becauſe his mercie is for euer.

notes.label: a
notes.text: VVhoſe goodnes is incomparable.

notes.label: b
notes.text: This ſecond part of euerie verſe, firſt pronounced by the Prieſtes, confeſſing & praiſing Gods mercie aboue al his workes, was ſtil repeted by muſicians, or other aſſiſtants, in maner as now in Litanies [ ô Lord deliuer vs ] and [ VVe beſech thee to heare vs ] And as Gloria Patri &c. is added in the end of Pſalmes, and our Lords prayer, and the Angelical ſalutation are often repeted in diuers Offices, and in the Roſarie.

verses.text: Confeſſe ye to <na>(c)</na> the God of goddes: becauſe his mercie is for euer.

notes.label: c
notes.text: VVhoſe diuine powre created al other thinges.

verses.text: <na>(d)</na> Confeſſe ye to <na>(e)</na> the Lord of lordes: becauſe his mercie is for euer.

notes.label: d
notes.text: By this inuitation to praiſe our Lord God, thriſe repeted, we profeſſe the Bleſſed Trinitie, who is one God in ſubſtance, and three Diuine Perſons.

notes.label: e
notes.text: VVhoſe dominion is ouer al the world.

verses.text: Who <na>(f)</na> onlie doth great meruels: becauſe his mercie is for euer.

notes.label: f
notes.text: Only God can do true miracles ; to wit, workes aboue the courſe of al nature.

verses.text: Who made the heauen <na>(g)</na> in vnderſtanding: becauſe his mercie is for euer.

notes.label: g
notes.text: In admirable wiſdom.

verses.text: Who eſtablished <na>(h)</na> the earth ouer the waters: becauſe his mercie is for euer.

notes.label: h
notes.text: Made the waters aboue nature to remaine vvithin their bondes, & not to couer the earth.

verses.text: Who made the great lightes: becauſe his mercie is for euer.
The ſunne to rule the day: becauſe his mercie is for euer.
The moone, and ſtarres to rule the night: becauſe his mercie is for euer.
Who ſtroke Ægypt with their firſtbegotten: becauſe his mercie is for euer. <cr>[1]</cr>
Who brought forth Iſrael out of the middes of them: becauſe his mercie is for euer.
In a mightie hand, and loftie arme: becauſe his mercie is for euer. <cr>[1]</cr>
Who diuided the Read ſea into diuiſions: becauſe his mercie is for euer.
And brought forth Iſrael through the middes therof: becauſe his mercie is for euer.
And he ouerthrew Pharao, and his hoſt in the Read ſea: becauſe his mercie is for euer. <cr>[1]</cr>
Who led his people through the deſert: becauſe his mercie is for euer. <cr>[1]</cr>
Who ſtroke great kinges: becauſe his mercie is for euer.
And ſlewe ſtrong kinges: becauſe his mercie is for euer.
Sehon the king of the Amorrheites: becauſe his mercie is for euer.
And Og the king of Baſan: becauſe his mercie is for euer.
And he gaue their land for an inheritance: becauſe his mercie is for euer.
For an inheritance to Iſrael his ſeruant: becauſe his mercie is for euer.
For in our humiliation he was mindful of vs: becauſe his mercie is for euer.
And he redemed vs from our enemies: becauſe his mercie is for euer.
Who geueth foode to <na>(i)</na> al fleshe: becauſe his mercie is for euer.

notes.label: i
notes.text: Al Gods benignitie, as wel of particular benefites towards his people, as general to them and al others procedeth from his mercie.

verses.text: Confeſſe ye to the God of heauen: becauſe his mercie is for euer. Confeſſe ye to the Lord of lordes: becauſe his mercie is for euer.

chapters.summary: God being meruelous in himſelf, 4. hath shewed his powre and goodnes in his workes, as wel in general to al the world, 10. as in particular towards his elected people. <na>[1]</na>

summary_notes.text:
God's marvelous works.
The 2. key.

verses.text: A Pſalme of Dauid <na>(a)</na> for Ieremie. VPON the riuers <na>(b)</na> of Babylon, there we <na>(c)</na> ſate and wept: whiles we <na>(d)</na> remembred Sion.

notes.label: a
notes.text: By adding to this title [ for Ieremie ] the Septuagint Interpreters ſignifie that this Pſalme treateth of the ſame captiuitie, in which Ieremias writte his Lamentations.

notes.label: b
notes.text: Nere the riuers in Chaldea ; wherof Babylon was the head citie,

notes.label: c
notes.text: the Iewes remained mourning,

notes.label: d
notes.text: remembring the holie rites and ſeruice of God, which had bene in Sion, wherof they were depriued in the captiuitie.

verses.text: On the willowes in the middes therof, we hanged vp <na>(e)</na> our inſtrumentes.

notes.label: e
notes.text: Al their muſical inſtruments, as hauing no vſe of them.

verses.text: Becauſe there they that led vs captiue, <na>(f)</na> demanded of vs wordes of ſonges. And they that led vs away: Sing ye an hymne to vs of the ſonges of Sion.

notes.label: f
notes.text: Either in earneſt, or in ſcorne the Chaldees willed them to ſing, as they were accuſtomed in their countrie.

verses.text: <na>(g)</na> How shal we sing the ſong of our Lord in a ſtrange land?

notes.label: g
notes.text: They excuſed themſelues, and refuſed to ſing ſacred Pſalmes before prophane people, neither had they mind to ſing in that mourning ſtate of captiuitie.

verses.text: <na>(h)</na> If I shal forget thee ô Ieruſalem, let my right hand be forgotten.

notes.label: h
notes.text: The people shew not only their feruent preſent deſire to ſerue God in Ieruſalem, but alſo their firme purpoſe ſtil to deſire the ſame, wiſhing that if they forget it, or loſe this affection, their right handes, or whatſoeuer is moſt deare, or neceſſarie for them, may be forgotten, not conſerued, but ſuffered to perish,

verses.text: <na>(i)</na> Let my tongue cleaue to my iawes, if I doe not remember thee: If I shal not ſet Ieruſalem in the beginning of my ioy.

notes.label: i
notes.text: If I loſe this affection, let me alſo loſe the vſe of my tongue.

verses.text: Be mindful ô Lord of <na>(k)</na> the childrem of Edom, in <na>(l)</na> the day of Ieruſalem: <na>(m)</na> That ſay: Raſe it, raſe it, euen vnto the foundation therof.

notes.label: k
notes.text: The Idomeans incenſed the Chaldees to be cruel againſt the Iewes, wherof they pray for iuſt reuenge, and withal the Pſalmiſt prophecieth that it wil be reuenged, which Iſaias alſo prophecieth, c. 21. v. 11.

notes.label: l
notes.text: for their reioycing in Ieruſalems miſerie.

notes.label: m
notes.text: The voice of the Idumeans, inciting the Babylonians vtterly to deſtroy Ieruſalem.

verses.text: <na>(n)</na> Daugther of Babylon miſerable: bleſſed is he, that shal repay thee thy payment, which thou haſt payed vs.

notes.label: n
notes.text: A prophecie that the people of Babylon should alſo be punished, for their crueltie againſt the Iewes, wherof Iſaias likewiſe prophecieth c. 13.

verses.text: Bleſſed is he, <na>(o)</na> that shal hold, and <na>(p)</na> shal dash thy litle ones againſt the rocke.

notes.label: o
notes.text: God wil bleſſe, or reward them that shal ſeuerly afflict the Babylonians,

notes.label: p
notes.text: not ſparing their children. Morally he is bleſſed, that mortifieth his owne paſſions, cutteth of firſt il motions, or punisheth venial ſinnes, that they grow not ſtrong within his ſoule, and ſo draw it to committe mortal ſinne. S. Aug. hic. & S. Greg in fine expoſ. Pſal. 4. pænit.

chapters.summary: The Prophet deſcribeth how lamentably the people in captiuitie of Babylon, wil bewaile the want of meanes to ſerue God, and of their natiue ſoyle : 7. with iuſt deſire of their enimies punishment. <na>[1]</na>

summary_notes.text:
The Jews' lamentation in captivity.
The 4. key.

verses.text: To <na>(a)</na> Dauid him ſelf. I wil <na>(b)</na> confeſſe to thee ô Lord in my whole hart: <na>(c)</na> becauſe thou haſt heard the wordes of my mouth. In <na>(d)</na> the ſight of Angels I wil ſing to thee:

notes.label: a
notes.text: This Pſalme is a fitte forme of thankes for Dauid, or anie other ſeruant of God.

notes.label: b
notes.text: I wil render thankes and praiſe.

notes.label: c
notes.text: God euer heareth the prayer that is rightly made, for which the ſupplicant is therfore to geue thankes.

notes.label: d
notes.text: Angels are preſent where the faithful pray, obſerue our prayers, and offer them to God, if they be ſincere, as the prayers of Tobias, and Cornelius.

verses.text: I wil adore <na>(e)</na> toward thy holie temple, and wil confeſſe to thy name. <na>[1]</na> For thy mercie, and thy truth: becauſe thou haſt magnified aboue euerie thing <na>(f)</na> thy holie name.

notes.label: e
notes.text: VVhen there was not acceſſe to the Temple, yet the Iewes praying in captiuitie, turned themſelues tovvards the Temple.

notes.label: f
notes.text: The Name and Maieſtie of GOD, The VVord (which is the Sonne of God) alſo the name of IESVS, is magnified aboue al names, or temporal thinges :

verses.text: In what day ſoeuer I shal inuocate thee, heare me: thou wilt multiplie ſtrength in my ſoule.
Let <na>(g)</na> al the kinges of the earth ô Lord confeſſe to thee: becauſe they haue heard al the wordes of thy mouth:

notes.label: g
notes.text: Sovvner or later Kinges and Princes of al kingdomes and nations, haue bene or ſhal be conuerted to Chriſt.

verses.text: And let them ſing in the wayes of our Lord: becauſe great is the glorie of our Lord.
Becauſe our Lord is high, and he beholdeth low thinges: and high thinges he knoweth <na>(h)</na> far of.

notes.label: h
notes.text: God knovveth proud men, not as his freindes or ſeruantes, but farre of, as ſtrangers and enimies.

verses.text: If I shal walke in the middes of tribulation, thou wilt quicken me: and vpon the wrath of mine enimies thou haſt extended thy hand, and thy right hand hath ſaued me.
Our Lord wil repay for me: ô Lord thy mercie is for euer: deſpiſe not the workes of thy handes.

chapters.summary: The whole Church, or anie iuſt perſon, rendreth thankes to God for his benefites 4. praying that al kinges and kingdomes may do the ſame, 6. becauſe God being high reſpecteth, and aduanceth the humble. <na>[1]</na>

summary_notes.text:
Thankes to God for benefites.
The 7. key.

verses.text: Vnto <na>(a)</na> the end, a Pſalme of Dauid. LORD thou <na>(b)</na> haſt proued me, and haſt knowen me:

notes.label: a
notes.text: By this part of the title [to the end] is ſignified (as is noted Pſal. 4.) that the matter conteined in the Pſalme, perteyneth to the newe Teſtament.

notes.label: b
notes.text: God vvho knovveth al thinges moſt abſolutly and perfectly, vvithout diſcourſe or ſearching, yet, as it vvere, maketh experimental trial of his ſeruants, to make them in ſome ſorte to know him, and to know themſelues. And ſo here, holie Dauid or other faithful man, acknowlegeth Gods Omniſcience, that is, perfect knovvlege of al thinges, without exception, paſt, preſent, & to come : al vvorkes, wordes, thoughtes, and whatſoeuer can be, though it neuer vvas nor ſhal be, in general and in particular.

verses.text: thou haſt knowen my ſitting downe, and my riſing vp.
Thou haſt vnderſtood my cogitations far of: my path, and <na>(c)</na> my corde thou haſt ſearched out.

notes.label: c
notes.text: The vttermoſt meaſure and reach of myne intention.

verses.text: And thou haſt foreſene al my wayes: becauſe there is not a word in my <na>(d)</na> tongue.

notes.label: d
notes.text: The word holden in by the tongue, and not vttered by mouth, is not hidden from God.

verses.text: Behold ô Lord thou haſt knowen al the laſt thinges, & them of old: thou haſt formed me, and haſt put thy hand vpon me.
Thy knowledge is <na>(e)</na> become meruelous of me: it is made great, and I can not reach to it.

notes.label: e
notes.text: By experiece we ſee that Gods knowlege exceedeth our reach.

verses.text: <na>(f)</na> Whither shal I goe from thy ſpirit? and whither shal I flee from thy face?

notes.label: f
notes.text: As Gods knowlege comprehendeth al thinges, ſo his preſence extendeth it ſelfe to al places, neither is conteined in place, but excedeth al place, in his diuine immenſitie.

verses.text: If I shal aſcend into heauen, thou art there: if I deſcend into hel, thou art preſent.
If I shal take my winges early, and dwel in the extreme partes of the ſea:
Certes thither alſo shal thy hand conduct me: and thy right hand shal hold me.
<na>(g)</na> And I ſayd: Perhaps darknes shal treade ouer me: and the night is mine illumination in my delightes.

notes.label: g
notes.text: The Prophet alſo in the perſon of anie curious imaginatiue man, examineth and findeth that no darknes, nor couer can hide anie thing from God.

verses.text: For darkenes shal not be darkened from thee, and the night shal be lightened as the day: as the darkenes therof, ſo alſo the light therof.
Becauſe thou haſt poſſeſſed <na>(h)</na> my reynes: thou haſt receiued me from <na>(i)</na> my mothers wombe.

notes.label: h
notes.text: Nothing ſemeth more hidden, then a mans entrals.

notes.label: i
notes.text: or a child in the mothers wombe.

verses.text: I wil confeſſe to thee, becauſe thou art terribly magnified: thy workes are meruelous, & my ſoule knoweth excedingly.
My <na>(k)</na> bone is not hid from thee, which thou madeſt in ſecrete: and my ſubſtance in the lower partes of the earth.

notes.label: k
notes.text: Or bones in the flesh.

verses.text: <na>(l)</na> Mine <na>[1]</na> imperfection thine eies haue ſene, & in thy booke <na>[2]</na> al shal be written: <na>(m)</na> daies shal be formed, & no man in them.

notes.label: l
notes.text: Or mans bodilie imperfection before his birth,

notes.label: m
notes.text: dayly formed by God, not by man. Iob. 10. v. 8. 2. Mac. 7. v. 21, 23.
Colem, Embryonem.
Of knowlege.

verses.text: <na>(n)</na> But to me thy <na>[1]</na> frendes ô God are become honorable exceedingly: their principalitie is exceedingly ſtrengthned.

notes.label: n
notes.text: Aboue al conſiderations it moſt excedeth, that God ſo high and infinite, honoreth his humble poore ſeruants ſo exceedingly, that it ſemeth to themſelues, farre more then can be due. For he rewardeth euen ouer & aboue merites ; which merites alſo are founded in Gods mercie geuen without merite.

Newe tranſlaters peruert this place, tranſlating [thoughts] for [frendes] contrarie to the Hebrevv, Greke, and Latin, and al ancient Fathers, only pretending, that the ſame word in the Chaldee tongue alſo ſignifieth thoughts.

verses.text: <na>(o)</na> I wil number them, and they shal be multiplied aboue the ſand: <na>(p)</na> I roſe vp and I am yet with thee.

notes.label: o
notes.text: The number alſo of Sainctes vvhom God hath choſen, called, iuſtified and vvil glorifie, excede mans conceipt. Apoc 7.

notes.label: p
notes.text: Incenſed with this excellent glorie, and deſiring to be of this innumerable multitude, by thy grace I haue riſen from ſinne, and in confidence of thy perpetual helpe, I ſtand and hope to perſeuere in thy ſeruice.

verses.text: <na>(q)</na> If thou shalt kil ſinners ô God: <na>(r)</na> ye men of blood depart from me.

notes.label: q
notes.text: And if it be ſo, yea ſeing it is ſo, that as thou ô God doeſt exalt thy Sainctes, to exceeding and vnſpeakable honour : ſo thou haſt alſo decreed to puniſh obſtinate ſinners, vvith eternal death and damnation :

notes.label: r
notes.text: I renounce al vvicked aſſociation, gette ye avvay from me al cruel bloudie men, that would drawe me into euerlaſting torments.

verses.text: <na>(s)</na> Becauſe you ſay in thought: they <na>(t)</na> shal receiue thy cities in vayne.

notes.label: s
notes.text: Away from me, you that thinke,

notes.label: t
notes.text: the glorious manſions in heauen, prepared and promiſed to the iuſt, are vaine hopes, and in vaine expected.

verses.text: <na>(v)</na> Did not I hate them, that hate thee ô Lord: and <na>(w)</na> pyned away becauſe of thine enemies?

notes.label: v
notes.text: This hate of ſuch ſinners the iuſt shal confidently plead, and happie are they that shal be able truly to alleage for themſelues in the day of iudgement, that they hated al, whom God hateth,

notes.label: w
notes.text: yea hated them vvith feruent zele, that are Gods enimies.

verses.text: <na>(x)</na> with perfect hatred did I hate them: they are become <na>(y)</na> enemies to me.

notes.label: x
notes.text: Stil the Prophet inculcateth this neceſſarie perfect hatred,

notes.label: y
notes.text: and enmitie towards Gods enimies.

verses.text: <na>(z)</na> Proue me ô God, and know my hart: examine me, and know my pathes.

notes.label: z
notes.text: For that none in this life (without ſpecial and extraordinarie reuelation) knoweth certainly their owne ſtate, whether they be worthie of Gods loue or hatred (Eccle. 9.) the iuſt ſubmitte themſelues to Gods examination of their hart and actions :

verses.text: And <na>(a)</na> ſee, if the way of iniquitie be in me: <na>(b)</na> and conduct me in the euerlaſting way.

notes.label: a
notes.text: humbly praing God, that if they be in the way of iniquitie,

notes.label: b
notes.text: he wil voutſafe to reduce and guid them into the right way of euerlaſting life.

chapters.summary: Gods knowlege, 7. and preſence (10. without the helpe, or hinderance anie thing) extendeth to al thinges, times, and places. 17. he geueth exceeding great honour to his ſainctes, 20. the wicked, as enimies to God are iuſtly hated, 23. the iuſt pray for Gods perpetual direction. <na>[1]</na>

summary_notes.text:
God's ſpecial providence of his ſervants.
The 3. key.

verses.text: Vnto the end, a Pſalme of Dauid.
DELIVER me ô Lord from the euil man: from the vniuſt man reſcue me.
Which <na>(a)</na> haue deuiſed iniquitie in their hart: <na>(b)</na> al the day they did appoint battels. They haue whet their tongues as that of a ſerpent:

notes.label: a
notes.text: Vnquiet euil diſpoſed men ſtil deuiſe wicked plottes,

notes.label: b
notes.text: and neuer ceaſe to make diſcord, and debates.

verses.text: the venome of aſpes is vnder their lippes.
Kepe me ô Lord from the hand of the ſinner: and from vniuſt men deliuer me.
Who haue deuiſed to ſupplant my ſteppes: the proude haue hid a ſnare for me: And they haue ſtreched out ropes for a ſnare: they haue layd <na>[1]</na> a ſtumbling blocke for me nere the way.

notes.text: ſcandalum.

verses.text: <na>(c)</na> I ſayd to our Lord: Thou art my God: heare ô Lord the voice of my petition.

notes.label: c
notes.text: In time of tentation prayer is moſt neceſſarie.

verses.text: O Lord, Lord <na>(d)</na> the ſtrength of my ſaluation: <na>(e)</na> thou haſt ouershadowed my head in the day of battel.

notes.label: d
notes.text: Man is not able to reſiſt temptations,

notes.label: e
notes.text: vnleſſe God by his grace, as by a helmet, defend him from yelding conſent.

verses.text: Yeld me not ô Lord from <na>(f)</na> my deſire, to the ſinner: they haue deuiſed againſt me, forſake me not, <na>(g)</na> leſt they perhaps be proude.

notes.label: f
notes.text: Suffer me not to fal from that which I now deſire (which is to be conſtant in vertue) not to conſent to ſinners perſwaſions.

notes.label: g
notes.text: VVho then would triumph ouer me.

verses.text: <na>(h)</na> The head of their compaſſe: <na>(i)</na> the labour of their lippes <na>(k)</na> shal couer them.

notes.label: h
notes.text: The ſumme of their miſcheuous deuiſes,

notes.label: i
notes.text: conſiſting in their ſubtle perſuaſions with ſwete wordes,

notes.label: k
notes.text: ſhal ouerwhelme, and bring themſelues to perdition.

verses.text: <na>(l)</na> Coales shal fal vpon them, <na>(m)</na> thou shalt caſt them downe into fyre: in miſeries <na>(n)</na> they shal not ſtand vp.

notes.label: l
notes.text: Hel fire shal be their lotes ;

notes.label: m
notes.text: into which they shal fal,

notes.label: n
notes.text: & euer be in intolerable torments.

verses.text: A man ful of tongue shal not be directed in the earth: euils shal take the vniuſt man into deſtruction.
<na>(o)</na> I haue knowne that our Lord wil do the iudgement of the needie: and the reuenge of the poore.

notes.label: o
notes.text: I haue learned by good inſtructions, and by experience, that in the end thou ô God wilt comfort the iuſt, who are now afflicted, and punish the vniuſt, that liue in temporal delightes, as it happened to Lazarus, and the glutton.

verses.text: But as for the iuſt, they shal confeſſe to thy name: and the righteous shal dwel with <na>(p)</na> thy countenance.

notes.label: p
notes.text: Eternal glorie conſiſteth in ſeeing God.

chapters.summary: The iuſt diuerſly afflicted by the wicked, pray to be defended, 7. repoſe their confidence in God, 10. who wil adiudge the reprobate to eternal punishment, 13. and reward the good with the fruition of himſelf. <na>[1]</na>

summary_notes.text:
Eternal pain of the wicked, and joy of the bleſſed.
The 10. key.

verses.text: A Pſalme of Dauid. LORD I haue cried to thee, heare me: attend to my voice, when I shal crie to thee.
<na>[1]</na> Let my prayer be directed as <na>(a)</na> incenſe in thy ſight: the eleuation of my handes as <na>(b)</na> euening ſacrifice.

notes.label: a
notes.text: As the ſume of incenſe is ſwete and aſcendeth vpwards : ſo the Church prayeth that her petitions may be gratful, and aſcend to God.

notes.label: b
notes.text: In the old teſtament morning ſacrifice was rather more ſolemne, and more frequent, but the Prophet ſemeth to allude vnto Chriſts Sacrifice, which he was to offer towards euening on the Croſſe ; and the ſame alſo in vnbloudie maner, the euening before his Paſſion, in the Euchariſt.
In theſe wordes the Church prayeth, offering incenſe in her ſolemne Offices.

verses.text: Set ô Lord <na>(c)</na> a watch to my mouth: and <na>(d)</na> a doore round about to my lippes.

notes.label: c
notes.text: A iuſt care and conſideration what to ſpeake, before the mouth be opened.

notes.label: d
notes.text: lippes muſt not be alwayes ſtopt, for it is a ſinne ſometimes not to ſpeake, but as a dore that is to be opened, and shut at due ſeaſons, for example ; opened to confeſſe our ſinnes, and Gods truth :

verses.text: Decline not my hart <na>(e)</na> into wordes of malice, to make excuſes in ſinnes. With men that worke iniquitie: and I wil not communicate with the chiefe of them.

notes.label: e
notes.text: shutte from wordes of malice, and from excuſing ſinnes committed.

verses.text: The iuſt shal rebuke me in mercie, and <na>(f)</na> shal reprehend me: but let not the oyle of a ſinner <na>(g)</na> fatte my head. Becauſe, <na>(h)</na> yet alſo my prayer is in their <na>(i)</na> good pleaſures:

notes.label: f
notes.text: Admonition of the iuſt, is a profitable reprehenſion,

notes.label: g
notes.text: but the fawning of flatterers is pernicious.

notes.label: h
notes.text: The Church ceaſeth not to pray for ſinners,

notes.label: i
notes.text: though as yet they take pleaſure in their ſinnes,

verses.text: <na>(k)</na> their Iudges are ſwalowed vp ioyned to the rocke. <na>(l)</na> They shal heare my wordes <na>(m)</na> becauſe they haue preuailed:

notes.label: k
notes.text: but the very chiefeſt of them, which ſeme moſt potent, if they remaine obſtinate to their death, shal then periſh, as men throwne againſt rockes.

notes.label: l
notes.text: They ſhal then heare and vnderſtand, that the prayers of the Church

notes.label: m
notes.text: are effectual, obtaining grace of conſtancie to her children, not to feare anie perſecution, nor anie kind of death ; obtayning alſo iuſtificatiô of their cauſe, vvhen the perſecuters shal ſee that the wordes, and doctrin of the Church are true, and preuaile in true iudgement, as true, modeſt, peaceable, not ſeditious, turbulent, nor againſt the commonwealth.

verses.text: <na>(n)</na> as the groſſenes of the earth is broken out vpon the earth. Our <na>(o)</na> bones are diſſipated <na>(p)</na> nere to hel:

notes.label: n
notes.text: As much earth ſticking together is made fructful, by breaking it into ſmal mould, ſo the children of the Church by perſecution, bring forth more fruict then before. S. Aug.

notes.label: o
notes.text: Some perſecuters are ſo cruel as to rage againſt the bones, and other reliques of Martyrs,

notes.label: p
notes.text: caſting them into the vileſt places they can, willing if they could, to throw them into hel,

verses.text: <na>(q)</na> for to thee ô Lord, Lord are mine eies; in thee haue I hoped, take not away my <na>[1]</na> ſoule.

notes.label: q
notes.text: but the Church and al her members repoſe confidence in God.
life.

verses.text: Keepe me from <na>(r)</na> the ſnare, which they haue ſet for me: and from <na>(s)</na> the ſcandals of them that worke iniquitie.

notes.label: r
notes.text: Therefore ſhe prayeth that her children be not entrapped by guilful deceiptes,

notes.label: s
notes.text: nor ouerthrowne by anie ſtumbling blocke caſt in their way.

verses.text: <na>(t)</na> Sinners shal fal in his net: <na>(v)</na> I am alone vntil I paſſe.

notes.label: t
notes.text: In the end, al perſecuters and other wicked shal be caught in their owne nette of perdition,

notes.label: v
notes.text: the Church is ſingularly protected euen to the end.
